issue: Redundant wording: 'a time you learned something new for the first time' — 'new' and 'for the first time' say the same thing
original_question: Tell a story about a time you learned something new for the first time.
suggested_rewrite: Tell a story about the first time you learned something that genuinely surprised you.

issue: Too vague to anchor a story — 'a pet or animal you've encountered' spans anything from your childhood dog to a squirrel; no moment or event is implied
original_question: Tell a story about a pet or animal you've encountered.
suggested_rewrite: Tell a story about a specific moment with an animal — a pet, a wild creature, anything — that made you feel something unexpected.
new_tips: Ground it in one specific moment, not a general description of the animal
Show what you felt in the moment, not just what happened
End with why the encounter stuck with you

issue: Asks user to 'illustrate the concept of resilience' — framing it as illustrating a concept turns it into a speech exercise, not a personal story; contradicts the mode
original_question: Tell a story that illustrates the concept of resilience, drawn from your own life.
suggested_rewrite: Tell a story about the hardest thing you've bounced back from. Don't name the lesson — let the story carry it.
new_tips: Pick the moment when you almost gave up, not the moment you recovered
Show the process of getting through it — the doubt, the small steps, the setback
Let the meaning emerge from the events, not from a stated theme

issue: Audience is contradictory: 'someone who has never used the internet' cannot realistically be the user of a smartphone app; the constraint makes the scenario implausible and blocks concrete delivery
original_question: Explain how a search engine works to someone who has never used the internet.
suggested_rewrite: Explain how a search engine works to an older relative who uses Google but has no idea what's happening behind the results.
new_tips: Start with what problem it solves: finding the right page among billions
Use an analogy they know, like a library index or a phonebook
Explain why results aren't random — someone decided that order

issue: No audience specified — the only prompt in the batch without a target listener; user has nothing to calibrate language or depth to
original_question: Explain how GPS navigation works on your phone.
suggested_rewrite: Explain how GPS navigation works on a phone to a curious friend who has always just assumed it's 'magic.'
new_tips: Start with satellites as the key idea — they're the hook that surprises most people
Explain triangulation without the word 'triangulation': three signals narrow a location
Tie it back to the user experience: why GPS still works when there's no cell signal

issue: No audience specified — the only finance prompt without a target listener; user has no calibration for vocabulary or depth
original_question: Explain how compound interest works and why it matters for saving money.
suggested_rewrite: Explain how compound interest works to a friend in their 20s who has never opened a savings account.
new_tips: Start with simple interest first, then show what changes when interest earns interest
Use a concrete number example with a small starting amount they can relate to
Show the long-term impact: what a 20-year difference in starting looks like

issue: Tip uses gendered pronoun 'she'll hear' for the CFO — inconsistent with the gender-neutral framing of all other prompts in the batch; a user whose CFO is male will find this jarring
original_question: Explain to your CFO why generative AI in your product is a strategic bet, not a feature, and why the cost is worth it.
suggested_rewrite: Explain to your CFO why generative AI in your product is a strategic bet, not a feature, and why the cost is worth it.
new_tips: Frame it as a unit-economics shift, not a capability — that's the language a CFO will hear
Pick one moat the bet creates and one risk it introduces; don't dilute with five
Close with the decision criterion you'd use in 18 months to know if it worked

issue: This is a persuasive argument to a CEO (negotiation/pitch territory), not an explanation of a concept; it has no audience who needs to understand something, only someone who needs to be convinced of a decision
original_question: Make the case to your CEO that your team needs three months to invest in technical foundations before adding new features, when revenue is up and the board wants velocity.
suggested_rewrite: Explain to your CEO what 'technical foundations' actually means and why teams that skip them slow down later — without using the phrase 'technical debt.'
new_tips: Translate the abstract into a physical analogy: what does building on shaky ground actually look like?
Connect it to a business outcome the CEO already cares about: speed of future features
Avoid using the ask as the explanation — the goal is understanding, not a decision

issue: This is a persuasive counter-argument (pitch/debate territory), not an explanation; 'Convince a board' is a rhetorical task, not an explanation task
original_question: Convince a board that the company should NOT integrate generative AI into its product right now, when every competitor just announced one.
suggested_rewrite: Explain to a board what the real risks of rushing a generative AI integration are, so they can make an informed decision — not just follow the competitive pressure.
new_tips: Lead with the cost they aren't seeing — quality risk, trust erosion — not the benefit they've heard
Use one concrete failure mode from a known product launch, not an abstract list
Frame the explanation as giving them better information, not telling them what to decide

issue: 'Convince a CFO' is a negotiation/persuasion task, not an explanation; the goal is a staffing decision, not audience understanding of a concept
original_question: Convince a CFO that the engineering team should hire two senior engineers at top-of-band salaries, instead of four mid-level hires for the same budget.
suggested_rewrite: Explain to a CFO why the output difference between senior and mid-level engineers is not linear — so they understand why the math of 'same budget, more people' doesn't hold.
new_tips: Reframe from headcount to output per quarter — that's the language a CFO will hear
Use one concrete example of work only seniors unblock, without insider jargon
Distinguish explanation from ask: your goal is their understanding, not their approval

issue: Tip uses gendered 'she' for the CEO — same issue as explanation_7-8_tech_005; inconsistent with all other prompts in the batch
original_question: Explain to a non-technical CEO why the engineering team needs to add latency to a feature, when every conversation so far has been about making it faster.
suggested_rewrite: Explain to a non-technical CEO why the engineering team needs to add latency to a feature, when every conversation so far has been about making it faster.
new_tips: Reframe latency as a property the CEO wants, not a cost they're paying — that single shift carries the explanation
Pick one specific failure mode the latency prevents, not a category
Avoid technical terms; the mechanism is what they need, not the vocabulary

issue: Asking a roommate to swap a chore is a simple social request, not a negotiation — no competing interests, no stakes, no pushback expected; feels out of place in a mode focused on persuasion under resistance
original_question: Ask your roommate to take over a chore you usually do this week because you have a big deadline.
suggested_rewrite: You and your roommate disagree about splitting a shared expense — you think it should be 50/50, they think it should reflect who uses it more. Work it out.
new_tips: Acknowledge the other person's logic before making your case
Propose a specific number or split, not just 'something fair'
Keep the relationship intact — this person still lives with you

issue: This is one-sided persuasion to a manager, not a two-party negotiation — there is no opposing interest to negotiate against, just a case to make; more suited to impromptu or pitch mode
original_question: Your team wants to push a product launch back by 2 weeks. Convince your manager this is the right call.
suggested_rewrite: Your manager wants to hold the launch date. You believe pushing it back two weeks will prevent a critical defect from shipping. Negotiate the delay while keeping trust intact.
new_tips: Acknowledge the cost of the delay to the manager before making your case
Quantify the risk of launching as planned — what specifically breaks?
Propose a compromise: what can you still ship on time to soften the ask?

issue: Mediating a dispute is a facilitation/coaching task, not a negotiation — the user is a neutral third party with no position to negotiate from; contradicts the mode's definition
original_question: You're mediating a dispute between two co-founders about the company's strategic direction. One wants to focus on enterprise, the other on consumer. Find a resolution.
suggested_rewrite: You are one of the co-founders. You believe the company must go enterprise. Your co-founder is pushing hard for consumer. Negotiate a direction you can both commit to.
new_tips: Identify shared goals before attacking the difference — both of you want the company to survive
Propose a framework for the decision, not just a compromise: what data would change your mind?
Address the emotional undercurrent: this disagreement is also about whose vision wins

issue: Tip 3 says 'Keep it under a minute' but targetDuration is 30 seconds — the tip contradicts the actual time constraint set for this prompt
original_question: If you could have dinner with any person, living or dead, who would it be and why?
suggested_rewrite: If you could have dinner with any person, living or dead, who would it be and why?
new_tips: Name the person in the first sentence — don't build up to the reveal
Pick one specific topic you'd want to discuss, not a general curiosity about them
End with what you'd take away from the conversation, not just what you'd say

issue: The prompt says 'You have 60 seconds' but targetDuration is 45 seconds — the stated time limit in the question text contradicts the actual session timer
original_question: You have 60 seconds. Convince someone to visit your hometown.
suggested_rewrite: Convince someone to visit your hometown. You have 45 seconds — make it count.
new_tips: Open with what makes your hometown unlike anywhere else — not its name or size
Hit one or two specific places, foods, or moments rather than a general list
End with an emotional hook: why would they regret not going?

issue: Prompt says 'You have 60 seconds to respond' but targetDuration is 60 seconds — the stated time limit is accurate but adding it inside the question text is redundant with the app's timer and feels awkward compared to other prompts in the mode
original_question: A friend says 'luck matters more than hard work.' Do you agree? You have 60 seconds to respond.
suggested_rewrite: A friend says 'luck matters more than hard work.' Do you agree or disagree? Take a clear position and defend it.
new_tips: State your position in the first sentence — no hedging
Use one specific example from your own life or someone you know
Acknowledge the strongest version of the opposite view before dismissing it

issue: Prompt says 'Give a 2-minute speech' but targetDuration is 90 seconds — stated duration contradicts the actual timer
original_question: You're given a random word: 'bridge.' Give a 2-minute speech that turns this word into a meaningful message.
suggested_rewrite: You're given a word: 'bridge.' In 90 seconds, build it into a meaningful message.
new_tips: Spend the first 5 seconds finding your angle — literal or metaphorical, not both at once
Build from the concrete meaning to a broader human truth
Land on something universal: what does 'bridge' reveal about people or decisions?

issue: The prompt tells the user to pick a topic they 'just made up on the spot,' but recorded in a solo app there is no 'on the spot' moment — the user sees the prompt before recording, which breaks the premise entirely
original_question: You have 90 seconds to explain why the person listening to you should care about a topic you just made up on the spot. Pick any topic and go.
suggested_rewrite: Pick the most obscure topic you genuinely know something about. In 90 seconds, make someone care about it.
new_tips: Name your topic in the first 3 seconds and commit — no second-guessing on camera
Use the rule of three: one hook, one surprising fact, one reason it matters to the listener
End with a question or provocation that stays with them after you stop talking

issue: The scenario asks the user to 'start a conversation naturally' but the tip says 'Open with an observation, not a question about their work' — this contradicts itself since the whole scene is set up around someone working; also unclear what the user should actually say
original_question: Introduce yourself to someone at a coffee shop who's working on their laptop. Start a conversation naturally.
suggested_rewrite: You're at a coffee shop and notice someone working on something that looks interesting. Open the conversation without asking what they're working on.
new_tips: Open with an observation about the space or moment, not the person's work
Share a brief, honest detail about yourself to give them something to respond to
Keep it light and easy to exit — they're working, not networking

issue: No scene or listener is specified — a pure pitch exercise with no networking context; the user has no one to pitch to and no setting, making it more of a presentation drill than a networking scenario
original_question: Deliver your 30-second elevator pitch: who you are, what you do, and what you're looking for.
suggested_rewrite: You're at a professional mixer and someone asks 'So, what are you working on these days?' Give your 30-second answer — make it feel like a real conversation, not a rehearsed pitch.
new_tips: Lead with the problem you solve or the thing you're building, not your job title
Make it specific enough to be memorable — 'marketing' is forgettable, 'helping restaurants fill tables on slow nights' is not
End with what you're looking for or curious about — give them an opening to respond

issue: 'Build rapport over the course of a conversation' — too open-ended; the user has no idea where to start, what to say, or what goal to pursue within 60 seconds; needs a clearer entry point
original_question: You're at an industry dinner and seated next to a potential mentor. Build rapport over the course of a conversation.
suggested_rewrite: You're at an industry dinner, seated next to someone 10 years ahead of you in your field. Open the conversation in a way that goes beyond small talk within the first two exchanges.
new_tips: Ask about their journey, not their title — 'How did you get into this?' beats 'What do you do?'
Find one genuine point of connection: a challenge you share, a project they've worked on
Share something real about yourself — rapport requires giving, not just asking

issue: Says '2 minutes at a podium' but targetDuration is 90 seconds — the stated and actual duration conflict
original_question: You have 2 minutes at a podium to introduce yourself to a room of 200 people at a conference. Make them want to talk to you afterwards.
suggested_rewrite: You have 90 seconds at a podium to introduce yourself to a room of 200 people at a conference. Make them want to find you during the break.
new_tips: Open with a hook that creates curiosity about you — not your title, your problem or perspective
Share one specific story or moment that reveals something they wouldn't find on your bio
Close with an invitation that makes approaching you feel easy and low-stakes
